explanations: terra: The covenant joins kindness to orphans and the needy with speaking good words to people, matching material vulnerability with a non-rebuking manner.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for عيل uses حرص for acquisitive greed; this verse uses أَحْرَصَ for people’s desire to live, even wishing for a thousand years. The changed object of desire cautions against reducing the source’s greed gloss to one wording or object.
terra: Hunger and loss of wealth are named as trials, making explicit both the bodily and material faces of the section's darlık.

luna: The section’s dictionary note calls the poor person a سائل; this verse pairs giving الْمَالَ with giving to the سَّائِلِينَ, alongside relatives, orphans, and the needy. It shows wealth moving toward the person who asks. | terra: True goodness includes giving beloved wealth to relatives, orphans, the needy, travelers, and ٱلسَّآئِلِينَ, the section's poor-as-asker made an object of care.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر identifies it as property; this verse uses تَرَكَ خَيْرًا for what a person leaves behind and directs a bequest from it. The legal context confirms the word’s material sense. | terra: إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا uses khayr for property left at death, the precise secondary sense of خَيْر developed in the section.

luna: The section develops the poor person as someone who asks and the enriched person’s encounter with him; this verse answers a question about spending by directing it to parents, relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers. It maps giving onto concrete relations and recipients. | terra: Asked what to spend, the verse calls the spendable property خَيْر and directs it to parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers.

luna: The section defines richness partly as having few needs and many possessions; when asked what to spend, this verse answers الْعَفْوَ, the surplus. It makes the boundary between sufficiency and excess a basis for giving. | terra: Asked what should be spent, the answer is the surplus beyond need, giving the section's idea of sufficiency a practical threshold.
terra: A father must provide a nursing mother's food and clothing reasonably, while no soul is burdened beyond capacity; household provision is fitted to means and need.
terra: A divorced woman receives provision according to the affluent person's capacity and the constrained person's capacity, making rich and poor subject to a measured duty.
terra: After calling for a good loan, the verse says God constricts and expands, locating both material straitness and abundance in the giver to whom all return.

luna: The section portrays sufficiency as something provided by another; this verse depicts wealth spent in God’s way as a seed multiplied many times over. It gives a concrete image of provision not being diminished by giving.

luna: The section commands that the asker not be rebuked; this verse describes spending wealth without following it with reminder or injury. It connects giving material support to preserving the recipient’s dignity.

luna: The section says not to drive away the سائل; this verse says a known kind word and pardon are better than charity followed by harm. It sets the dignity of the petitioner above the giver’s display of payment. | terra: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, and God's being غَنِىٌّ frames how the former needy person should receive a petitioner.

luna: The section’s instruction not to rebuke the asker has a direct boundary here: charity is nullified by reminders and injury. The verse shows how a gift can fail to relieve need when the giver humiliates its recipient.
terra: The command to spend from the good things one has earned and not select the bad makes concrete the section's “abundant and cleanly acquired” sense of wealth; God is غَنِىٌّ.

luna: The section describes need answered by enrichment from فضل; this verse says Satan يَعِدُكُمُ الْفَقْرَ while God promises forgiveness and bounty. It names fear of poverty as a pressure that can turn a person away from giving. | terra: Satan promises poverty and urges indecency, while God promises forgiveness and bounty; it exposes fear of want as the seed of grasping.

luna: The section shows that need can be concealed: restrained poor people may be mistaken for rich. This verse says that concealing charity while giving it to the poor is better, a specific way of meeting need without making the recipient’s exposure the point. | terra: Hidden charity given to the poor is called better for the donors, joining material aid, khayr, and restraint from exposing the recipient.
terra: Whatever khayr people spend returns fully to them, using “good” for spendable property while directing it toward the needy context completed in 2:273.

luna: The section’s dictionary note says a poor person may be called a سائل; this verse describes needy people whose restraint makes the uninformed count them as rich, and says they do not ask insistently. It prevents the reader from equating visible asking with the whole condition of poverty. | terra: The restrained poor are mistaken for أَغْنِيَآءَ and do not ask insistently, sharpening the section's identification of a poor person with a sā'il by showing the silent case.
terra: God effaces usury and makes charities grow, opposing acquisitive increase to the kind of giving through which wealth truly bears fruit.
terra: A debtor in hardship must receive respite until ease, and remission is better, turning financial straitness into a claim on the creditor's mercy.
terra: The disbelievers' wealth and children will not تُغْنِىَ عَنْهُم before God, so worldly abundance cannot meet the decisive need.

luna: The section names acquisition greed as a trace of want; this verse says righteousness is not attained until one spends from what one loves. It marks the inward attachment to wealth and the action that loosens it. | terra: People do not attain true goodness until they spend from what they love, making prized property into khayr only through release rather than possession.
terra: Pilgrimage binds duty to human ability, then declares God غَنِىٌّ عَنِ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ; creaturely capacity is measured while God needs none of it.
terra: Again wealth and children cannot suffice before God, reinforcing the limit on possessions as a source of independence.

luna: The section says enrichment comes through another’s hand, not a self-awarded status; this verse condemns people who withhold what Allah gave them from His bounty while thinking it good for them. It directly opposes receiving wealth and then treating it as grounds to keep it from others. | terra: Those stingy with what God gave from His bounty think it good for them, but the withheld property becomes a collar, denying that possession itself is khayr.
terra: The claim إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ فَقِيرٌ وَنَحْنُ أَغْنِيَآءُ blasphemously reverses the creaturely poverty and divine richness stated in 35:15.
terra: Property is called a means of support established by God; dependents are to be fed, clothed, and addressed kindly from it, uniting material sufficiency with humane speech.
terra: The rich guardian must abstain while the poor guardian may consume reasonably, making wealth and poverty determine a measured use of another's property.

luna: The section depicts the poor petitioner at someone’s door and forbids harshness; this verse says that when relatives, orphans, and needy people are present at an inheritance division, they should be given something and addressed graciously. It supplies a concrete setting for receiving need with generosity.
terra: Those who consume orphan property unjustly are consuming fire into themselves, reversing the former orphan's obligation to make possession serve rather than prey on vulnerability.
terra: Good conduct is required toward orphans, the needy, near and distant neighbors, companions, and travelers, widening the doorstep encounter with need.

luna: The section ends with the blessing to be spoken of; this verse condemns miserliness and concealing what God gave from His bounty. It gives concealment of received provision as the opposite response to recognizing a blessing.
terra: If spouses separate, يُغْنِ ٱللَّهُ كُلًّا مِّن سَعَتِهِ promises that God can make each sufficient from His abundance.
terra: After affirming God's ownership of heaven and earth, the verse names Him rich and praiseworthy, grounding independence in universal possession.
terra: Justice must not bend for either rich or poor because God is closer to both, preventing material status from controlling moral judgment.
terra: Feeding ten needy people from the average food of one's household gives material “enoughness” a measured legal form.

luna: The section’s dictionary says wealth is called خَيْر only when it is abundant and from a good source; this verse states that bad and good are not equal even if كَثْرَةُ الْخَبِيثِ impresses you. It marks abundance alone as no proof of good or clean wealth.
terra: God يُطْعِمُ وَلَا يُطْعَمُ: He feeds and is not fed, the provider's independence set against every creature's need.
terra: وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ ذُو ٱلرَّحْمَةِ joins the section's Rabb and ghani roots: the need-free Lord possesses mercy and can replace creatures without depending on them.

luna: The section includes fear of want answered by divine enrichment; this verse forbids killing children مِّنْ إِمْلَاقٍ and answers that God provides for parents and children. It makes feared poverty within a household a direct case of provision coming from beyond the household.
terra: God establishes people on earth and places livelihoods there, yet they give little thanks, tracing means of living to the provider rather than acquisition alone.
terra: The أصحاب الأعراف ask the proud rich what their gathering and arrogance أَغْنَىٰ for them, exposing accumulated company or property as failed sufficiency.
terra: God reminds a once weak and fearful community that He sheltered, supported, and provided them good things, a collective movement from vulnerability to sufficiency.
terra: At Hunayn the believers' great numbers do not تُغْنِ عنهم شيئًا, extending the boundary of sufficiency from possessions to human abundance.

luna: The section’s dictionary form عيلة names want; this verse places believers’ fear of عَيْلَةٍ beside God’s promise يُغْنِيكُمُ from His bounty. It turns the image of one person made sufficient into a communal fear of lost livelihood answered by divine provision. | terra: This is the exact Qur'anic reprise of the image: feared عَيْلَة is answered by God's future يُغْنِيكُم from His bounty.

luna: The section describes wealth and acquisitive greed; this verse condemns hoarding gold and silver without spending in God’s way. Neighboring 9:35 gives the consequence of that hoarding, while this ayah identifies the withholding itself. | terra: Religious authorities consume people's property wrongfully and hoard gold and silver instead of spending it, combining corrupt acquisition with refusal to answer need.

luna: The section describes wealth as a provision that can free another from need; this verse says the hoarded gold and silver are heated and used to mark their owners. Neighboring 9:34 identifies the hoarding, and this ayah reverses retained wealth into bodily punishment. | terra: The hoarded metal is heated and used to brand its owners, turning stored wealth into the bodily mark of the greed named in 9:34.
terra: Contentment with nearer life over the Hereafter is rebuked because worldly enjoyment is little, reinforcing the image's better-latter scale.
terra: Some people are pleased with the distribution of charity only when they receive a share and angry when they do not, staging need transformed into entitlement rather than contentment.

luna: The section connects the poor person to the asker and to wealth; this verse names the poor and needy among the recipients of alms. It specifies a communal route by which wealth reaches people in want. | terra: Obligatory alms are assigned first to ٱلْفُقَرَآءِ and the needy, showing wealth deliberately moved into the hands of those lacking it.
terra: A person promises charity and righteousness if God gives from His bounty, staging poverty's hoped-for transition before 9:76 tests it.
terra: Once God gives from His bounty, they become stingy and turn away, showing received sufficiency converted into acquisitive withholding.
terra: The poor donors who لَا يَجِدُونَ إِلَّا جُهْدَهُمْ give the little they can find, joining the “find/means” sense with generosity under constraint.
terra: There is no blame on those who لَا يَجِدُونَ مَا يُنفِقُونَ, a direct case in which not “finding” means lacking property to spend.
terra: Those denied mounts because the Prophet can find none leave weeping that they lack anything to spend, embodying unmet material need without acquisitive pride.
terra: Charity taken from people's property purifies and causes growth, answering the section's concern with wealth's clean source and use.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss links عيل to حرص in the sense of acquisition; this verse calls the Messenger حَرِيصٌ عَلَيْكُم, concerned for you, then describes his compassion. It marks a distinct, benevolent sense of the wording rather than acquisitive greed.
terra: God is هُوَ ٱلْغَنِىُّ and owns all in heaven and earth, so the two definitions of richness—absence of need and possession—coincide fully in Him.
terra: Every creature's provision rests with God, universalizing the section's relation between the needy being and the one who places sustenance in its reach.
terra: The deities invoked besides God do not أَغْنَتْ عَنْهُم when the Lord's command arrives, marking false providers as unable to meet decisive need.
terra: Jacob says his protective plan cannot أُغْنِى عَنكُم مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ, distinguishing prudent means from the one whose decree ultimately suffices.
terra: Joseph's brothers arrive afflicted with hardship and scant goods, ask for full measure and charity, and thus stage needy petition before one able to supply.

luna: The section moves from want to sufficiency and places خير against the Hereafter; this verse says Allah expands and measures provision, then contrasts rejoicing in worldly life with its small share beside the Hereafter. It joins changing livelihood to the surah’s scale of what is truly better. | terra: God expands and measures provision, and worldly life is only a brief enjoyment beside the Hereafter, joining material measure to 93:4's scale of better things.

luna: The section closes by telling the recipient of نعمة to speak of it; this verse joins gratitude for God’s favor with the promise of increase. It frames received sufficiency as a gift to acknowledge rather than a self-made status. | terra: Gratitude for blessing is answered with increase, so acknowledged provision grows rather than becoming a title of self-sufficiency.
terra: Even universal ingratitude leaves God غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ, so acknowledged blessing benefits the receiver rather than supplying a need in the giver.
terra: God gives from all that people ask and His نعمة cannot be counted, yet the human is deeply ungrateful; asking, gift, and acknowledgment meet.
terra: God places livelihoods on earth both for people and for creatures they do not provide for, making hidden provision broader than human ownership.
terra: What the people of the Stone had earned did not أَغْنَىٰ for them, a concise reversal of acquisition imagined as security.

luna: The section places need and blessing together; this verse says every نعمة people have is from Allah, then says they cry to Him when harm touches them. It links received good living to the same dependence exposed by hardship. | terra: Every نعمة is from God, and distress makes people cry to Him; comfortable living is explicitly traced back to its giver.

luna: The section traces poverty becoming wealth and asks the reader to see the giver behind it; this verse says God has favored some over others in provision, then depicts those favored withholding it from those under their authority. It makes unequal provision and refusal to share visible.
terra: People recognize God's niʿmah and then deny it, the reverse of recounting the comfortable livelihood one has received.
terra: What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, setting accumulated holdings against lasting sufficiency.

luna: The section’s dictionary account of نعمة points to ease and good living; this verse describes abundant provision arriving from every place, followed by the taste of hunger and fear when the people deny God’s blessings. It stages comfort and deprivation as opposite conditions. | terra: A town once secure with abundant provision denies God's favors and is made to taste hunger and fear, reversing niʿmah's pleasant livelihood into bodily want.
terra: People are to eat the lawful, good provision God supplied and thank His niʿmah, joining nourishment, clean provision, and acknowledgment of its source.

luna: The section’s petitioner is someone in need; this verse commands giving the relative, needy person, and traveler their due. It turns the encounter with need into an allotted right, and its warning against waste sets a limit on the giver’s use of wealth. | terra: The relative, needy person, and traveler are each to receive their due, directly staging the encounter between a possessor and someone in need.
terra: If one must turn the needy away while awaiting provision from the Lord, one must still speak gently; this specifies how not to rebuff the petitioner of 17:26.

luna: The section defines richness partly through having little need, and identifies acquisitive greed as a trace of want; this verse warns against both a closed hand and spending everything, which leaves a person blamed and destitute. It gives the image a boundary of measured use. | terra: The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended completely, because either extreme ends in blame or destitution; spending is calibrated around enoughness.

luna: The section depicts poverty answered by enrichment; this verse states that the Lord expands الرِّزْقَ for whom He wills and measures it for whom He wills. It locates both abundance and constraint within the same act of provision. | terra: The Lord expands and measures provision for whom He wills, locating both plenty and straitness in the provider's knowledge.

luna: The section names fear of poverty in 9:28 and God’s enrichment from bounty; here the fear is that children will bring إِمْلَاقًا, and God says He provides for them and their parents. It applies the same fear-and-provision relation to future need.

luna: The section identifies acquisitive greed as an inward trace of want; this verse says that even if people held the treasuries of their Lord’s mercy, they would withhold them for fear of spending, and that humanity is miserly. It gives a direct counterpoint to sufficiency received and passed on. | terra: Even owners of God's treasuries would withhold for fear of spending; imagined abundance fails to cure the fear of lack.
terra: The garden owner boasts that he has more wealth and a stronger following, treating comparative possession as a self-made rank.
terra: The garden owner enters while wronging himself and declares that his property will never perish, mistaking present acquisition for lasting sufficiency.
terra: He doubts the Hour and assumes that even a return to God would bring him something better, carrying material entitlement beyond death.
terra: His companion tells him to acknowledge God's will and power even if the companion has less wealth and children, relocating sufficiency in the giver.
terra: The garden's produce is destroyed and its owner wrings his hands over what he spent, making accumulated wealth visibly pass away.
terra: After the garden's loss, no party can help him besides God and he cannot help himself, exposing the social following of 18:34 as failed sufficiency.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر can mean wealth; this verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life, then says the enduring good deeds are better. It distinguishes material “good” from what remains with God. | terra: Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while lasting good deeds are خَيْر with the Lord in reward and hope; it pairs 93:4's “better” with possessions that pass.
terra: The boat belongs to poor people who work at sea, showing that “poor” can describe unmet need even when the poor possess a productive asset.
terra: Abraham asks why his father serves what cannot hear, see, or يُغْنِى عَنكَ شَيْـًٔا, exposing an alleged provider that can supply no need.
terra: The promise that one will neither hunger nor be unclothed marks a boundary state in which the bodily signs of poverty are absent.
terra: The Prophet must not covet others' temporary splendor because وَرِزْقُ رَبِّكَ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, joining better provision to what remains.
terra: Sacrificial food is to be given to ٱلْبَآئِسَ ٱلْفَقِيرَ, joining bodily nourishment to an emphatic description of the poor person's distress.
terra: The sacrificial animals feed both the content or non-asking poor person and the one who approaches to ask, refining the section's poor-as-sā'il category.
terra: Because everything in heaven and earth belongs to God, He is ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ; possession and independence coincide only for the universal owner.
terra: The question asks whether wealth and sons are mistaken for God's hastening خَيْرَات to their owners, challenging property read as assured good.
terra: كَل لَّا يَشْعُرُونَ rejects that inference, bounding visible plenty as neither moral good nor proof of favor.
terra: People of bounty and means must continue giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants and must pardon, so abundance is defined by what it enables them to pass on.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss links عائل to poverty and أَغْنَى to making someone sufficient; here فقَرَاءَ are promised that Allah may يُغْنِهِم from His bounty. The same movement is applied to households formed by marriage. | terra: The poor are brought into a household through marriage and God promises يُغْنِهِمُ ٱللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ, matching sufficiency placed in another's hand.
terra: Those who do not يَجِدُونَ means for marriage must remain chaste until God يُغْنِيَهُم; it joins the section's “finding” and “enriching” senses beside 24:32.

luna: The section contrasts want, sufficiency, and acquisitive greed; this verse describes the faithful as neither extravagant nor miserly, but balanced between them. It makes sufficiency a measured relation to wealth rather than its maximum accumulation. | terra: The servants neither squander nor stint, but keep spending between those extremes, directly expressing wealth governed by measure rather than acquisitive fear.
terra: Long enjoyment does not أَغْنَىٰ when punishment arrives, marking temporal plenty as unable to secure lasting welfare.
terra: Gratitude benefits oneself, while disbelief cannot diminish the Lord who is غَنِىٌّ كَرِيمٌ; true richness is joined to generosity.
terra: At Midian's water Moses finds two women holding back their animals because their father is old; this is the needy scene his act in 28:24 answers.

luna: The section’s dictionary account of خَيْر includes wealth, while Moses says he is فَقِيرٌ to whatever good God sends down. In context he has just watered the two women’s flock and withdrawn to the shade, so the verse makes need after useful labor and immediate shelter concrete. | terra: After watering the women's flock, Moses says he is فَقِيرٌ for any خَيْر God sends; need, beneficial provision, and the provider are all explicit.
terra: One woman returns with an invitation to reward Moses for watering, showing provision arriving immediately after the confession of poverty in 28:24.
terra: The proposal to hire Moses turns his strength and trustworthiness into livelihood, one concrete way the prayer of 28:24 is answered.
terra: Work and marriage are joined in the father's offer, so the needy stranger is given both livelihood and household after 28:24.
terra: Those fearing dispossession are reminded that they were established in a secure sanctuary to which fruits are brought as provision, answering fear of loss with supplied security.
terra: Whatever people are given is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, the same scale that places lasting good above present property.
terra: Qarun's immense treasuries and exultation stage wealth as acquisitive excess rather than enoughness received with humility.
terra: Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him and to do good as God did good to him, turning received property into transmitted benefit.
terra: Qarun claims the wealth was given because of knowledge he possesses, the narrative form of taking conferred richness as a self-bestowed title.
terra: Those desiring worldly life envy Qarun's mighty fortune, showing how visible acquisitions awaken the soul's craving.
terra: The knowledgeable answer that God's reward is better, restoring the “better latter” scale against Qarun's displayed wealth.
terra: Qarun and his house are swallowed, and no party can help him, so possessions and status fail as sufficiency.
terra: The former admirers recognize that God expands and measures provision and that worldly success does not prove divine favor.

luna: The section shows the poor man as someone unable to meet his needs; this verse pictures creatures that do not carry their provision and says Allah provides for them and for people. It places sufficiency in provision received rather than in the creature’s stockpiling. | terra: Many creatures cannot carry their own provision; God provides for them and for people, making dependence on the giver visible.

luna: The section depicts a poor petitioner meeting someone who has been enriched; this verse commands giving relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due, and connects that act with seeking God’s face. It is another direct formulation of wealth moving toward need. | terra: Kin, the needy, and the traveler are to receive their due, presenting held property as containing claims belonging to vulnerable others.
terra: Wealth advanced to increase through others' property does not grow with God, while alms given for God are multiplied; it separates grasping increase from fruitful giving.
terra: Wisdom directs gratitude because it benefits the grateful person, whereas God remains غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ, separating received blessing from the giver's need.
terra: The people of Sheba are told to eat their Lord's provision and thank Him, presenting good livelihood as a gift to be acknowledged.
terra: When they turn away, the two fruitful gardens are replaced by bitter, sparse produce; comfortable provision reverses into insufficiency.
terra: The affluent boast of greater wealth and children and infer that they will not be punished; 34:37 rejects possession as spiritual rank.
terra: God expands and measures provision as He wills, denying that material abundance is self-produced or an unqualified mark of favor.
terra: Wealth and children do not bring anyone near to God; possession is bounded as neither spiritual sufficiency nor self-bestowed rank.

luna: The section glosses enrichment as making someone sufficient; this verse says that what people spend, God replaces, and names Him the best of providers. It directly joins expenditure to provision returned by the giver. | terra: God expands or measures provision and promises to replace whatever is spent, answering the fear that giving will create poverty.

luna: The section defines richness as freedom from need; this verse reverses the scale by declaring people فقَرَاءُ إِلَى اللَّهِ and God الْغَنِيُّ الْحَمِيدُ. It makes material sufficiency one case within humanity’s deeper dependence. | terra: أَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ and God's being ٱلْغَنِىُّ make creaturely need and true independence face one another.
terra: Those told to spend God's provision refuse by asking whether they should feed someone God could feed, exposing a false appeal to the provider used to rebuff the needy.
terra: In its immediate context al-khayr names prized horses whose love distracts from remembrance, a concrete property-sense that shows valued possession becoming attachment.
terra: God is rich beyond people's need, yet approves gratitude rather than disbelief, separating the giver's independence from the receiver's duty to acknowledge blessing.
luna: The section glosses أَغْنَى as making someone sufficient; this verse asks whether Allah is not كَافٍ عَبْدَهُ. It states sufficiency through God’s care rather than through possessions.
terra: What earlier peoples earned did not أَغْنَىٰ for them, opposing acquired gain to the sufficiency only the giver can secure.
terra: The former nations' greater power and earnings do not أَغْنَىٰ for them, another direct limit on acquisitions as sufficiency.

luna: The section’s dictionary form سائل means a poor petitioner; this verse says provision on earth is سَوَاءً لِّلسَّائِلِينَ. If سائلين here means those who ask or seek provision, it extends the link from a petitioner at a door to provision made available to seekers; that lexical bridge is uncertain. | terra: The earth's sustenances are measured سَوَآءً لِّلسَّآئِلِينَ; if “those who ask” here includes creatures seeking provision, it widens the poor-as-sā'il image to universal dependence.

luna: The section identifies acquisitive greed as one trace of want; this verse says unrestricted expansion of provision would make people transgress, while God sends it down by measure. It explains why abundance is not simply multiplied without limit. | terra: Unlimited provision would make people transgress, so God sends it down in a measured amount; sufficiency is distinguished from acquisitive excess.
terra: Worldly gifts are temporary enjoyment, but what is with God is خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ, distinguishing holdings from lasting sufficiency.
terra: God apportions livelihoods and ranks in worldly life, while the Lord's mercy is better than what people accumulate; need, measure, and acquisitions meet in one verse.
terra: The luxurious niʿmah in which Pharaoh's people delighted is among what they leave behind, making comfortable abundance visibly pass away.
terra: No protecting relation can يُغْنِى one person from another on the decisive day, bounding social dependence as a form of sufficiency.
terra: Neither their earnings nor adopted protectors يُغْنِى عَنْهُم, showing that possessions and dependencies alike can fail the need they promise to meet.
terra: In a call to spend, stinginess harms the miser himself because وَٱللَّهُ ٱلْغَنِىُّ وَأَنتُمُ ٱلْفُقَرَآءُ; this joins poverty, divine sufficiency, and acquisitive withholding.

luna: The section connects the poor person with the سائل at the door; this verse says that in the wealthy people’s أَمْوَالِهِمْ is a right لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ. It makes the asker a claimant to wealth, not merely an interruption to its owner. | terra: Their wealth contains a recognized right لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ, placing the asker and the deprived at the possessor's door.
terra: People's provision and what they are promised are said to be in heaven, locating sufficiency beyond the visible holdings in their hands.
terra: God desires no provision from creatures and does not ask them to feed Him, denying every mark of need in the giver.
terra: God is ٱلرَّزَّاقُ, possessor of power, completing 51:57's contrast between the provider and those who must be provided for.

luna: The section glosses أَغْنَى as making another sufficient; this verse names God as the one who أَغْنَىٰ and أَقْنَىٰ, so sufficiency and the giving of possessions have an agent beyond the recipient. | terra: أَغْنَىٰ وَأَقْنَىٰ names God as both the giver of wealth and the giver of enduring possessions, exactly the section's two definitions of riches.
terra: People are asked why they do not spend when the inheritance of heaven and earth belongs to God, denying that temporary custody makes wealth independently theirs.
terra: The good loan to God is multiplied for its giver, turning property released from the hand into greater provision rather than feared loss.

luna: The section’s ayah 93:4 says the Hereafter is better than the first life, while its dictionary discussion turns to material wealth; this verse depicts rivalry in wealth and children as part of worldly life and contrasts it with the Hereafter. It makes material abundance part of a passing order. | terra: Worldly life becomes rivalry in multiplying wealth and children before its growth withers, making acquisitions visibly abundant and passing.
terra: Those who are stingy and command stinginess are answered by God's being ٱلْغَنِىُّ ٱلْحَمِيدُ, true independence confronting hoarded wealth.
terra: Wealth and children will never تُغْنِىَ عَنْهُم before God, denying the richest household ultimate independence.

luna: The section defines riches partly through possessions; this verse directs distribution so wealth will not be دُولَةً among the rich alone. It sets a boundary against the concentration that would leave the poor outside sufficiency. | terra: The allocation includes orphans, the needy, and the traveler so property will not circulate only بَيْنَ ٱلْأَغْنِيَآءِ, giving the social consequence of wealth placed in one's hand.
terra: The distributed property is specifically for poor emigrants expelled from homes and possessions, a concrete state of need beside 59:7's limit on rich-only circulation.
terra: The hosts prefer the migrants over themselves وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ, turning one's own scarcity away from the acquisitive greed the section names.
terra: People are told to spend from God's provision before death makes them wish for one more chance to give charity, setting passing possession against its lasting use.
terra: People reject the messengers and turn away, while وَّٱسْتَغْنَى ٱللَّهُ; the reflexive “self-sufficiency” that is false for the grasping human is true of God.
terra: The command to listen, obey, and spend is joined to rescue from one's own shuhh, directly naming the inward greed that can survive material plenty.
terra: A good loan to God is multiplied and forgiven, another direct answer to acquisitive fear that spending diminishes sufficiency.

luna: The section glosses أَغْنَى as making someone sufficient; this verse says that whoever relies on Allah finds that He is حَسْبُهُ, and joins that sufficiency to provision from an unexpected source. | terra: Provision comes from where the servant does not reckon, God is enough for the one who trusts Him, and He has set a measure for everything.
terra: Housing is required مِن وُجْدِكُم, according to one's means, a Qur'anic use of the “finding” root for material capacity close to the source dictionary sense.

luna: The section defines wealth as sufficiency; this verse tells the person of ample means to spend from that means and the one whose provision is restricted from what God gave him, then promises ease after hardship. It measures obligation to actual provision rather than imagined abundance. | terra: The affluent and the constrained each spend from what God has given, and سَيَجْعَلُ ٱللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا states the movement from straitness to ease.
terra: Even marriage to two righteous servants does not يُغْنِيَا the disbelieving wives before God, showing that a household relation cannot confer ultimate sufficiency.
terra: People walk the earth and eat from God's provision, so ordinary livelihood is received from a domain made usable by the provider.
terra: The challenge asks who could provide if God withheld His provision, defining dependence by imagining the provider's gift removed.
terra: The owners of a garden are tested when they resolve to harvest in the morning, beginning a scene in which possession meets the poor person's claim.
terra: A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, making the hidden giver's power to remove provision decisive before their exclusion of the poor.
terra: Their plan is that no needy person enter the garden, a direct reversal of welcoming the poor person who arrives at one's provision.
terra: They go out determined to withhold, showing acquisitive resolve immediately before their imagined sufficiency collapses.
terra: On seeing the ruined garden they say they are مَحْرُومُونَ, becoming the deprived people they had meant to exclude.
terra: They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better, returning failed possession to dependence on the giver.
terra: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنِّى مَالِيَهْ is the ruined person's admission that property did not suffice, a direct boundary on monetary ghina.
terra: The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor, making neglect of hunger a failure with lasting consequence.

luna: The section describes want’s spiritual trace as acquisitive greed; this verse says the human being was created impatient or anxious. Neighboring 70:20–21 specify the responses to harm and good that make this disposition relevant to poverty and provision. | terra: The human is described as anxiously grasping, introducing the inward disposition that appears as panic in want and withholding in plenty.

luna: The section traces want into an inward condition; this verse says that when evil touches a person he becomes anxious. Neighboring 70:21 supplies the opposite response when good reaches him—he withholds—completing a specific need-and-abundance pattern. | terra: When harm touches him he becomes frantic, the scarcity-side of the acquisitive disposition completed in 70:21.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss links poverty with acquisitive greed; this verse says that when good touches the person, he withholds. Neighboring 70:20 gives his anxiety under harm, making the two verses a direct reversal between deprivation and received good. | terra: When good touches him he withholds, turning received plenty into the soul-level greed the section identifies as poverty's trace.

luna: The section connects enrichment with wealth and the poor petitioner; this verse says the faithful have a known right in their wealth. Neighboring 70:25 identifies its recipients as the asker and the deprived, completing the claim. | terra: The worshippers' wealth contains a known right, so possession is presented as carrying an obligation rather than conferring independence; 70:25 names its recipients.

luna: The section’s dictionary note calls the poor person a سائل; this verse names لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ as recipients of the known right in wealth. Neighboring 70:24 supplies the claim that this right is held within their wealth. | terra: لِّلسَّآئِلِ وَٱلْمَحْرُومِ names both the asking poor person and the one deprived without asking, completing 70:24's rule for wealth.
terra: أُو۟لِى ٱلنَّعْمَةِ names affluent people of ease who deny, using the niʿmah root in precisely the section's secondary sense of comfortable living.
terra: Whatever khayr people send ahead for themselves is found with God as better and greater in reward, moving valuable property from present possession to lasting return.
terra: God identifies the wealthy opponent as one He created alone, placing his later abundance against his original utter dependence.
terra: God says He placed extensive wealth in the man's hand, explicitly identifying another as the source of his possessions.
terra: Children kept present around the wealthy man add household and social capital to the wealth and ease God says He placed in his hand.
terra: God says He made life smooth for him, matching the section's definition of niʿmah as ease and pleasant living.
terra: After extensive wealth and ease, the man still covets increase, a precise instance of plenty failing to end acquisitive need.
terra: The condemned confess that they did not feed the needy, another direct reversal of letting received provision answer another's want.

luna: The section moves from receiving sufficiency to encountering a poor person; this verse describes feeding the مسكين, orphan, and captive despite love for the food. It makes a response to need an act of giving from what one values. | terra: They give food, despite loving or needing it, to a needy person, orphan, and captive, answering hunger without treating possession as self-sufficiency.
terra: The smoke's shade neither shelters nor يُغْنِى مِنَ ٱللَّهَبِ, extending the agnā-as-suffice sense to a physical provision that fails its basic purpose.
terra: Frowning begins a scene of receiving a vulnerable visitor badly, the enacted opposite of not rebuking the petitioner.
terra: The reason for the frown is that the blind man came to him; this identifies the visitor whose reception 80:1 judges.
terra: The person who ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ receives attention, making presumed self-sufficiency the social status preferred over the vulnerable visitor.
terra: Giving oneself eagerly to the self-sufficient person completes the misplaced preference introduced in 80:5.
terra: The other person comes striving, an active seeker whose approach helps specify the vulnerable visitor of the rebuke scene.
terra: Being distracted from the earnest visitor completes the reversal of the command not to drive away the one who comes asking.
terra: People prefer the nearer life, identifying the preference that 87:17 and 93:4 correct.
terra: وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ directly matches the surah's claim that the latter is better while adding that it remains.
terra: The food of punishment neither nourishes nor يُغْنِى مِن جُوعٍ; the sufficiency sense of the source's agnā branch is denied at the exact point of hunger.

luna: The section follows poverty and enrichment as a change in condition; here a person whose Lord أَكْرَمَهُ وَنَعَّمَهُ concludes, “my Lord has honored me.” The neighboring 89:16 gives the inverse conclusion under restricted provision, and 89:17–20 correct the equation of wealth with honor. | terra: When his Lord honors him and gives him نعمة, the human calls himself honored; the verse directly tests the section's link between niʿmah and comfortable living.

luna: The section traces want becoming sufficiency; here provision is قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ and the person concludes, “my Lord has humiliated me.” The neighboring 89:15 supplies the opposite economic state, while 89:17–20 reject both status judgments as a measure of care for the poor. | terra: When his provision is measured tightly, the human says his Lord has humiliated him; it marks the boundary between material straitness and true worth.
terra: كَلَّا rejects that inference and identifies the real failure as not honoring the orphan, reversing the conduct commanded around the poverty image.

luna: The section says not to rebuke the سائل; this verse condemns failing to urge طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ. It turns the response to need from mere restraint in speech toward active concern; 89:17 names the adjacent failure to honor the orphan. | terra: Failure to urge feeding the poor makes neglect of bodily need, rather than restricted provision itself, part of the preceding moral diagnosis.
terra: Consuming inheritance wholesale turns acquired property into predation, the corrupt counterpart to wealth received and shared as provision.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for عيل includes حرص, acquisitive greed; this verse says people love الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا. Its surrounding neglect of the poor makes that appetite a social harm, not just an inward feeling. | terra: Loving wealth with consuming love gives a Qur'anic form to the acquisitive craving that the section calls poverty's trace in the soul.

luna: The section names poor nutrition as a bodily trace of want; this verse pictures feeding during a day ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ, severe hunger. Neighboring 90:15–16 specify the vulnerable people reached by that response. | terra: Feeding on a day of مَسْغَبَة confronts hunger as the bodily form of poverty; 90:15–16 identify who is fed.

luna: The section’s image concerns a person’s need and the response to someone arriving for help; this verse identifies a near orphan as one recipient in the passage’s feeding response. Neighboring 90:14 supplies the day of hunger and 90:16 names the needy person in misery. | terra: An orphan of near kin is the first person named in the feeding scene, linking material sufficiency to the surah's neighboring care for the orphan.

luna: The section says the poor person may be a سائل; this verse names a مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ, a needy person in misery, as the next recipient in the feeding passage. Neighboring 90:14 supplies the hunger setting and 90:15 the orphan. | terra: مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ depicts the needy person reduced to dust, the concrete recipient of the food in 90:14.
terra: The one who gives and remains mindful stands opposite the grasping “self-sufficient” person introduced in 92:8.
terra: God promises to ease the giver toward ease, a neighboring promise that makes 92:8's self-sufficiency part of a moral fork.

luna: The section explicitly contrasts its verb أَغْنَى—wealth received through another—with this person who is بَخِلَ and اسْتَغْنَىٰ, treating himself as self-sufficient. The contrast exposes the difference between being enriched and claiming independence. | terra: The miser بَخِلَ وَٱسْتَغْنَىٰ claims independence through withholding, the precise reversal of being made sufficient by another in 93:8.
terra: The miser is eased toward hardship, reversing the movement from poverty to sufficiency and completing the consequence of 92:8.
terra: وَمَا يُغْنِى عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ denies that his wealth will suffice when he falls, exposing false self-sufficiency in the very agnā sense the section develops.
terra: Human transgression is the consequence stated immediately before the person's seeing himself as self-sufficient in 96:7.

luna: The section contrasts divine enrichment with self-awarded sufficiency; here the human being’s seeing himself اسْتَغْنَىٰ leads to transgression. The verse marks self-sufficiency as a dangerous misreading of wealth. | terra: أَن رَّءَاهُ ٱسْتَغْنَىٰ makes self-perceived independence, rather than received sufficiency, the cause of rebellion.
terra: The return is to the Lord, immediately bounding the human's claim in 96:7 that he has become self-sufficient.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for خَيْر includes wealth, and its gloss for عيل includes acquisitive حرص; this verse joins الْخَيْرِ to intense love. In context it names the human pull toward wealth that the section’s greed gloss diagnoses. | terra: The human's fierce حُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ uses khayr for wealth and exposes attachment to acquisition rather than measured sufficiency.
terra: Competition for increase distracts people, reducing the “many acquisitions” definition of wealth to a hunger that never becomes enough.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for نعمة describes comfort and good living; this verse says people will be asked about النَّعِيمِ. It adds accountability to the comfort whose arrival the section calls a blessing.
terra: The slanderer gathers wealth and repeatedly counts it, a compact portrait of acquisitive craving.
terra: He thinks his wealth makes him last, mistaking possession for lasting sufficiency.

luna: The section names malnutrition as poverty’s bodily trace; this verse says the Lord fed Quraysh مِن جُوعٍ and secured them from fear. It gives bodily hunger a direct counterpart in divine provision. | terra: The Lord of the House أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ, a compact image of a provider removing the bodily mark of poverty.

luna: The section’s whole-surah context pairs the former orphan’s care with restraint toward the asker; this verse condemns forcefully driving away the orphan. It shows the opposite treatment of a vulnerable person once need is no longer one’s own. | terra: The denier يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ, a direct reversal of the surrounding surah's commands not to overpower or rebuff the vulnerable visitor.

luna: The section says not to rebuke the سائل; this verse condemns failing to urge food for the مسكين. It makes disregard for the poor a boundary against the section’s dignified response to need. | terra: Not urging the food of the poor turns the bodily need behind the image into the test the denier fails.
terra: مَآ أَغْنَىٰ عَنْهُ مَالُهُۥ وَمَا كَسَبَ denies sufficiency to both held wealth and acquisition.
